claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre mice have no effect on viability.
source: By comparing littermate Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre (phenotypically WT control) and Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre (mutant) mice, we observe that eliminating Wls in a subset of neural progenitors with Gfap-Cre has no effect on viability
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript based on observation of mice

claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre mice have a ~25% reduction in body size and weight at early post-weaning ages that decreases to a ~5% reduction by six weeks of age.
source: eliminating Wls in a subset of neural progenitors with Gfap-Cre has no effect on viability but is associated with (i) a ~ 25% reduction in body size and weight at early post-weaning ages that decreases to a ~ 5% reduction by six weeks of age
evidence: Direct observation and measurement of body size and weight in mutant mice

claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre mice exhibit male infertility.
source: eliminating Wls in a subset of neural progenitors with Gfap-Cre has no effect on viability but is associated with (i) a ~ 25% reduction in body size and weight at early post-weaning ages that decreases to a ~ 5% reduction by six weeks of age and (ii) male infertility.
evidence: Direct observation of reproductive phenotype in mutant mice

claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains show absence of the corpus callosum.
source: Examination of the principle cortices, tracts, and nuclei revealed only two visible alterations in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains: (i) absence of the corpus callosum
evidence: Direct observation from DAPI/cresyl violet staining and uDTI imaging

claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains show a large reduction in the size of the dentate gyrus.
source: Examination of the principle cortices, tracts, and nuclei revealed only two visible alterations in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains: (i) absence of the corpus callosum and (ii) a large reduction in the size of the dentate gyrus (DG).
evidence: Direct observation from DAPI/cresyl violet staining and uDTI imaging

claim: In some Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains the DG appears to be almost completely missing.
source: In some Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains the DG appears to be almost completely missing, whereas, in others, the most ventral (i.e., posterior) region of the hippocampus retains the DG at a reduced size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation from histological sections shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In some Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains, the most ventral region of the hippocampus retains the DG at a reduced size.
source: In some Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains the DG appears to be almost completely missing, whereas, in others, the most ventral (i.e., posterior) region of the hippocampus retains the DG at a reduced size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation from histological sections shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: DGCs are largely missing from Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains.
source: Visualizing DG granule cells and mossy cells by immunostaining for Prox1 and calretinin, respectively, showed that DGCs are largely missing from Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains whereas DG mossy cells are retained (Figure 1C, left).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C

claim: DG mossy cells are retained in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains.
source: Visualizing DG granule cells and mossy cells by immunostaining for Prox1 and calretinin, respectively, showed that DGCs are largely missing from Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains whereas DG mossy cells are retained (Figure 1C, left).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Mossy fibers are lost in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains.
source: Consistent with this pattern of cell body loss, visualizing mossy fibers, the axons of the DGCs that synapse onto CA3 pyramidal cells, by immunostaining for Calbindin showed a corresponding loss of mossy fibers in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Gfap-Cre is expressed in the medial and dorsal cerebral cortex by embryonic day E14.5.
source: This analysis revealed Gfap-Cre expression in the medial and dorsal cerebral cortex by embryonic day (E)14.5, including the cortical hem, an organizing center for hippocampal development that is located at the most medial edge of the developing cortex (Figure 2A; Grove et al., 1998).
evidence: Reporter analysis shown in Figure 2A and cited reference

claim: The cortical hem is an organizing center for hippocampal development located at the most medial edge of the developing cortex.
source: This analysis revealed Gfap-Cre expression in the medial and dorsal cerebral cortex by embryonic day (E)14.5, including the cortical hem, an organizing center for hippocampal development that is located at the most medial edge of the developing cortex (Figure 2A; Grove et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited reference Grove et al., 1998

claim: In some tissues, expression of LEF1 is induced by beta-catenin signaling as part of a presumptive positive feedback loop.
source: To assess the spatiotemporal pattern of beta-catenin signaling, we took advantage of the observation that in some tissues, such as CNS endothelial cells, expression of the beta-catenin partner LEF1 (also known as LEF/TCF), is induced by beta-catenin signaling as part of a presumptive positive feedback loop (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited reference Wang et al., 2019

claim: LEF1 levels in the cortical hem are similar in both Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre and Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains at E14.5.
source: Immunostaining for LEF1 shows the highest intensity in the cortical hem with similar levels in both Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre and Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains at E14.5 (Figure 2A, upper panels).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A

claim: At E15.5, LEF1 levels in the cortical hem are markedly lower in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre compared to Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains.
source: However, at E15.5, LEF1 levels in the cortical hem are markedly lower in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre compared to Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains (Figure 2A, lower panels).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The cellular architecture of the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre cortex appears normal, including the abundance and locations of Cajal–Retzius cells.
source: Despite the reduced LEF1 level, the cellular architecture of the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre cortex appears normal, including the abundance and locations of Cajal–Retzius cells, which are important for normal DG development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Hodge et al., 2013).
evidence: Observation from Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and cited reference

claim: Cajal–Retzius cells are important for normal DG development.
source: Despite the reduced LEF1 level, the cellular architecture of the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre cortex appears normal, including the abundance and locations of Cajal–Retzius cells, which are important for normal DG development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Hodge et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited reference Hodge et al., 2013

claim: At E18.5, LEF1 accumulation is localized to the region of the future DG in control Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains.
source: At E18.5, a time when the mature hippocampal architecture is recognizable, LEF1 accumulation is localized to the region of the future DG in control Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains (Figure 2B, upper panels)
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B

claim: At E18.5, the analogous territory in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains contains fewer cells and shows greatly reduced LEF1 levels.
source: but the analogous territory in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains contains fewer cells and shows greatly reduced LEF1 levels (Figure 2B, lower panels).
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Beta-catenin signaling drives cell proliferation in many normal developmental contexts and in neoplasia.
source: In many normal developmental contexts, as well as in the context of neoplasia, beta-catenin signaling drives cell proliferation
evidence: General scientific knowledge about beta-catenin signaling

claim: The number of EdU-positive cells in the region that gives rise to the DG was reduced ~5 fold in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains compared to Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains at E18.5.
source: In support of this idea, the number of EdU-positive cells in the region that gives rise to the DG, marked by Prox1 immunostaining, was reduced ~5 fold in Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brains compared to Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains at E18.5 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: EdU labeling and quantification shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: The number of EdU-positive neural progenitors in the adjacent hippocampal migratory stream showed less than a 2-fold difference between Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre and Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains.
source: By contrast, the number of EdU-positive neural progenitors in the adjacent hippocampal migratory stream showed less than a 2-fold difference.
evidence: EdU labeling and quantification shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: Immunostaining for cleaved Caspase-3 showed minimal cell death in both Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre and Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains at E17, E18.5, and P0.
source: Immunostaining for cleaved Caspase-3 showed minimal cell death in both Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre and Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre brains at E17, E18.5, and P0 (data not shown).
evidence: Immunostaining data (not shown in figures)

claim: The nearly complete absence of DGCs in the adult Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brain reflects a failure to produce these cells during development rather than production followed by loss.
source: We conclude that the nearly complete absence of DGCs in the adult Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre brain reflects a failure to produce these cells during development rather than production followed by loss.
evidence: Inference from EdU and Caspase-3 data

claim: 60 transcripts with reduced abundance in the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre hippocampus met the criteria of fold change >3 and false discovery rate < 0.05.
source: The RNAseq data revealed 60 transcripts with reduced abundance in the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre hippocampus that met the criteria of fold change (FC) >3 and false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05.
evidence: Bulk RNAseq analysis results

claim: 55 of the 60 transcripts with reduced abundance in the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre hippocampus are specifically expressed or substantially enriched in DGCs.
source: Strikingly, 55 of the 60 transcripts are specifically expressed or substantially enriched in DGCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: Bulk RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: 34 transcripts met the FC and FDR criteria for increased abundance in the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre hippocampus.
source: The bulk RNAseq analysis also revealed 34 transcripts that met the FC and FDR criteria for increased abundance in the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre hippocampus.
evidence: Bulk RNAseq analysis results

claim: 27 of the 34 transcripts with increased abundance in the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre hippocampus are specifically expressed in the choroid plexus.
source: Twenty-seven of these transcripts are specifically expressed in the choroid plexus (black dots; Figure 3A, left panel), and, therefore, their presence likely indicates choroid plexus contamination in the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre hippocampus samples during dissection.
evidence: Bulk RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3A and inference about contamination

claim: DGCs comprise 32% of the Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre nuclei (4306 of 13,523).
source: As summarized in the percentile plot in Figure 3B, DGCs comprise 32% of the Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre nuclei (4306 of 13,523)

source: As summarized in the percentile plot in Figure 3B, DGCs comprise 32% of the Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre nuclei (4306 of 13,523) but only 3.5% of the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre nuclei (548 of 15,573).
evidence: snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Inhibitory neurons comprise 9% of the Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre nuclei and 15.5% of the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre nuclei.
source: All other neuronal cell types show increased cell numbers in the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre data set, with the greatest increases seen for (1) inhibitory neurons, which comprise 9% of the Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre nuclei and 15.5% of the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre nuclei

claim: Excitatory neurons other than CA1, CA2, CA3 pyramidal cells comprise 8% of the Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre nuclei and 21% of the Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre nuclei.

claim: The reduction in the abundance of DGCs should produce a 1.3-fold increase in relative abundance for all non-DGCs.

claim: Only two transcripts fulfilled the criteria of FC >2 with a q-value <0.05 for differential expression: Trps1 and Cntnap5a, both in a subset of excitatory neurons.

claim: DGC axons constitute the mossy fiber bundle.
source: DGC axons, which constitute the mossy fiber bundle, project to the CA3 region where they form synapses with both pyramidal cells and inhibitory interneurons (Jaffe and Gutiérrez, 2007).
evidence: Cited reference Jaffe and Gutiérrez, 2007

claim: DGC-pyramidal cell synapses are composed of en passant presynaptic boutons from DGC axons and complex postsynaptic spines on the proximal dendrites of CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: DGC-pyramidal cell synapses are composed of en passant presynaptic boutons from DGC axons and complex postsynaptic spines on the proximal dendrites of CA3 pyramidal cells (Rollenhagen and Lübke, 2006).

claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre CA3 pyramidal cell morphologies appear unaffected by visual inspection.
source: By visual inspection, Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre CA3 pyramidal cell morphologies appear unaffected, and there were no significant differences in the lengths of apical or basal dendrites between genotypes (Figure 4A and B).

claim: There were no significant differences in the lengths of apical or basal dendrites between Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre and Wlsfl/+;Gfap-Cre CA3 pyramidal cells.

claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre CA3 pyramidal cells show a modest and statistically significant reduction in the mean density of complex spines on apical dendrites.

claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre CA3 pyramidal cells show a modest and statistically significant reduction in the mean density of simple spines on basal dendrites.

claim: Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre CA3 pyramidal cells have normal morphologies but exhibit a modest reduction in the number of synaptic spines.
source: Based on these analyses, we conclude that Wlsfl/-;Gfap-Cre CA3 pyramidal cells have normal morphologies but they exhibit a modest reduction in the number of synaptic spines – in particular, a modest reduction in the density of and coverage with complex spines on apical dendrites – an effect that may be secondary to the large reduction in DGC inputs.
evidence: Summary of Golgi staining and stereological analyses

claim: No systematic differences were seen between the sexes in behavioral testing.
